title: Use of AI in Law Enforcement: The Present and Future Prospects
abstract: This chapter provides an exploration of the intersection between artificial intelligence (AI) and the evolving landscape of law enforcement in the context of financial crimes. It offers a detailed examination of the transformative impact of AI technologies on traditional investigation techniques. The chapter begins with an overview of the need to integrate AI tools, as emerging technologies expand, in law enforcement. Through a series of case studies inspired by the TRACE project, the authors illustrate how AI is reshaping law enforcement practices, from crime analytics to the use of knowledge graphs. Key themes include an analysis of the operational benefits derived from AI, such as enhanced investigative capabilities, resource optimisation, and improved decision-making processes. The ethical considerations inherent in the use of AI in law enforcement are carefully dissected, addressing issues of bias, privacy concerns, and the need for transparency and accountability. By delving into the challenges and opportunities presented by AI adoption, the chapter offers a nuanced understanding of the complex dynamics at play. Policymakers, law enforcement professionals, and academics will find this work to be a valuable resource, providing insights into the responsible integration of AI to augment public safety efforts.

title: AI, Law and Ethics in Countering Financial Crime
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the fight against financial crime, but how can it be deployed responsibly? In answer to that question, this book provides a comprehensive roadmap that integrates legal clarity, ethical guidance, and operational strategies on AI governance. Leveraging the EU's AI Act, national legal instruments and comparative insights, the book examines the challenges of AI governance and offers practical tools for bias mitigation, explainability, accountability, and risk management. The book's use of real-world case studies and contributions from academics and practitioners – including experts with law enforcement experience – enables scholars, students, and professionals in disciplines such as law, criminology, finance, and policing to bridge theory and practice. This makes it an indispensable resource for research, teaching, and professional training. Whether you are shaping policy, implementing compliance frameworks, or exploring AI's role in fighting financial crime, this book provides the roadmap you need to balance innovation and responsibility. This title is also available as open access on Cambridge Core.

title: Review of: "MedAgentBench: A Realistic Virtual EHR Environment to Benchmark Medical LLM Agents"
abstract: The authors build MedAgentBench, a benchmark for LLM agents acting inside an electronic health record.The pieces are: 300 tasks written by two internal medicine physicians who are also authors (Section 2.1), 100 deidenti ed Stanford patient pro les carrying 785,207 records in total (Table 2, row "Number of records (total)"), a HAPI FHIR JPA server packaged as a Docker image (Section 2.3), and a small orchestrator that exposes nine FHIR functions and caps each episode at 8 rounds (Section 2.4.3).Twelve models are scored under pass@1 with task success rate as the only metric (Section 2.4.1).The headline result is Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 at 69.67% overall (Table 3, row "Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2", column "Overall SR"), which the authors read as an unsaturated benchmark with room to grow.The artifact is the real contribution here, and it is a good one: a FHIR-shaped environment plus clinician-written tasks is exactly what this eld has been missing.My concerns are almost entirely about the measurement layer stacked on top of it.Two things I checked rst, because reviewers often ag them wrongly.Table 2 adds up: 563,426 Observation + 124,969 Procedure + 74,821 Condition + 21,991 MedicationRequest = 785,207, matching the stated total exactly.And Table 3 is internally coherent: with 150 query and 150 action tasks (Section 2.5.1),every row's Overall SR is the mean of its Query SR and Action SR to rounding, and every row of Table 4 reproduces its Overall SR under group sizes of 90 easy, 120 medium, 90 hard.The bookkeeping is careful.The inferential claims built on it are not.

title: Review of: "DRC-Coder: Automated DRC Checker Code Generation Using LLM Autonomous Agent"
abstract: The paper tackles a real and unglamorous problem: every new technology node forces engineers to hand-write an integrated (grid-based) DRC checker that agrees with the signoff commercial tool, and that takes weeks of reading foundry documents and debugging.DRC-Coder automates it with two GPT-4o agents in an AutoGen group chat -a Planner that turns the foundry rule description plus layout images into grid-domain conditions, and a Programmer that writes the Python drc function -plus three tool functions (Foundry Rule Analysis, Layout DRV Analysis, DRC Code Evaluation, Section 4).The third one is the engine of the method: it runs the candidate code over a dataset of 207 NVCell standardcell layouts (Section 3.1) and reports precision, recall, F1, and a summary of false positives/negatives back to the agents, which then iterate.The headline claims are F1 = 1.000 on all seven design rules versus F1 = 0.631 for standard prompting, 2.3 debugging iterations, and 210 seconds per rule (Section 5.2).The framing and the engineering are good, and the domain-speci c evaluation function is the part I would keep.The evidence, as reported, does not yet support the strength of the claims -mainly because the loop that produces the code optimizes directly on the metric that is then reported, and because the version I am reviewing does not contain the main results table at all.A note on the version I received I am reviewing exactly the text as it appears on the Qeios article page.In that rendering, the body of Table 1 is missing.The caption for Table 1 is present (immediately before Section 5: "Performance evaluation of DRC code generation using standard prompting and our DRC-Coder with GPT-4o and Llama3 across seven design rules… Precision (P), Recall (R), and F1 score (F) for each method… the Qeios qeios.com

title: Agentic AI for Digital Product Passport Documentation: A Feasibility Study on Heterogeneous Manufacturing Documents
abstract: Digital Product Passports (DPPs) are intended to make lifecycle product information accessible across the value chain and enable circular business models. Yet, the adoption remains constrained by the heterogeneity of existing industrial documentation and the cost for normalizing it into unified schemes. Agentic systems based on large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative path that operates directly on existing documents rather than restructuring them. This paper presents a feasibility study combining a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review (SLR) of 23 agentic document-reasoning systems with a small-scale empirical evaluation of one system on a purposive sample of 204 questions across the documents of 12 industrial and consumer products. The aim of the study is to generate qualitative insights about where current capabilities are sufficient and where they fall short. The system answered 85% of questions correctly, with 5% incomplete and 10% false. Two patterns emerge consistently. First, the reasoning capabilities of the frontier model appeared adequate for industrial document understanding. The practical bottleneck, for the single frontier model and orchestration pattern evaluated here, lay in retrieval, where general-purpose embeddings failed to bridge the terminological gap between user queries and manufacturer-specific vocabulary. Second, deterministic tools markedly improved the answer quality in question categories, where LLMs are structurally weakest. These observations suggest that the retrieval infrastructure adapted to manufacturer vocabulary and complementary deterministic tools may be more consequential design priorities for DPP deployments supported by agentic AI than further work on orchestration complexity.

title: Auditing what was said: the epistemic promise and limits of ambient AI in clinical practice
abstract: Traditional audits based on written charts may overlook aspects of clinical reasoning that shape patient care. Ambient artificial intelligence enables systematic analysis of clinician–patient dialogue at scale. We report a hypothesis-generating analysis of 124 single-centre urology consultations. A transcript-centred audit revealed inter-physician variation and expert disagreement that were not captured by chart review alone. We examine its epistemic value alongside its nonverbal, behavioural, technical, and regulatory limitations.

title: Analysis of The Performance of Artificial Intelligence-Based Language Models in Electrical and Electronics Education Exam Questions
abstract: Over the last decade, advances in artificial intelligence have begun to transform educational practices. With the development of OpenAI's ChatGPT, it has become clear that AI chatbots' capabilities—such as generating human-like text, facilitating automated conversations, and answering questions—will have widespread impact across various sectors, including education and healthcare. Consequently, the use of chatbots in various applications has accelerated. Today's most popular chatbots, OpenAI ChatGPT and large language models (LLMs) like Google Gemini and Bard, are making significant progress with applications in various fields, including electrical and electronics education. In this study, the performance of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), ChatGPT (GPT-5.1), Bard and Gemini was analyzed in answering 240 carefully prepared questions in Turkish language using clear, specific and plain text formats to determine knowledge levels, covering 12 sub-specialties in the field of electrical and electronics. Two experts analyzed the accuracy metric in the performance analysis, and the results are presented comparatively. The statistical significance of the findings was also determined, and it was observed that there were significant differences for the exam evaluations of some courses.

title: Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into everyday systems, understanding how users perceive and interact with AI is critical for effective design. This systematic literature review analyzes 1,565 peer-reviewed scholarly articles published post-2023 from IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, and Web of Science, ultimately including 33 publications that met the inclusion criteria. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, this review examines how user trust in AI-enabled systems is defined and measured, and which interaction design factors influence it. The findings reveal that the literature reflects diverse contributions from authors, institutions, and disciplines, while also employing varied definitions and methodologies, contributing to a fragmented body of work. In addition, this review identifies nine key design factors, including explainability, anthropomorphism, confidence, interface, errors, security, transparency, competence, and perceived control. Overall, greater consensus within the field is needed to support the development of stronger and more cohesive bodies of work for each design factor.

title: Quantifying scholars’ marginal contributions to average-based journal metrics
abstract: Abstract Attributing journal metrics to individual scholars is essential for modeling research influence, yet current methods rely on a restrictive assumption of monotonicity. Traditional credit allocation frameworks, such as Full and Fractional counting, assume that adding a research article to a portfolio never decreases a scholar’s attributed standing. While valid for cumulative metrics, this logic is mathematically inconsistent with average-based metrics like the Journal Impact Factor (JIF). Such indicators are inherently non-monotonic functions where performance below the established mean exerts a reductive impact on the aggregate score. This study challenges the monotonic baseline by introducing a marginal attribution framework that captures how individual marginal contributions can either increase or decrease an average-based journal metric. We propose three novel methods: Marginal Full Credit , Marginal Fractional Credit , and Marginal Shapley . The latter adapts the game-theoretic Shapley value using an average-based characteristic function to calculate marginal contributions that may be negative. To ensure scalability for large datasets where exact computation is prohibitively complex, we employ a statistically rigorous and commonly used bounded Monte Carlo approximation. Empirically, we test these methods on a dataset of articles from twelve leading Information Science journals. Our findings demonstrate that, because citation distributions are highly right-skewed, over 50% of scholars are associated with negative signed marginal effects on the journal-period average. These values should not be interpreted as penalties or judgments of scholarly quality; rather, they are a structural inevitability of average-based indicators and reflect the mechanical behavior when publication-level citation rates fall below the relevant journal mean. By relaxing the monotonicity constraint, this study aligns attribution models with the mathematical reality of scholarly metrics, providing a nuanced understanding of how individual output shapes collective performance indicators.

title: BioOps : Enabling MLOps for scalable and flexible model‐centric process control in biopharmaceutical development
abstract: The deployment of advanced modeling and machine learning in biopharmaceutical process control has been limited by legacy fragmented automation infrastructure and a lack of model lifecycle governance. We present BioOps, a modular automation framework for biopharmaceutical advanced process control (APC). The framework incorporates established Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) principles, including version-controlled model registries, containerized deployment, and continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. BioOps explicitly decouples model development from model execution within the control architecture. This decoupling enables process scientists to deploy, test, and iteratively refine mathematical models and control strategies in a flexible manner. These workflows can be applied across heterogeneous bioreactor platforms and are executed entirely in-house, without reliance on vendor-specific solutions or custom system integration. In addition, BioOps embeds traceability, auditability, and model lifecycle management directly into the control stack. As a result, the framework aligns with regulatory expectations while continuing to support agile, in-house experimentation and development. Case studies across a geographically distributed set of bioreactors demonstrate BioOps' versatility in PAT-driven feedback control, hybrid model-based nutrient and glucose feeding, adaptive phase transitions, and cross-scale deployment. By operationalizing model-centric control through an MLOps-inspired architecture, BioOps provides a practical foundation for scalable, reproducible, and future-ready biomanufacturing.

title: Review of: "AgentNet: Decentralized Evolutionary Coordination for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems"
abstract: The paper proposes AgentNet, a multi-agent framework in which every LLM agent carries both a router and an executor, so that task allocation happens through local peer-to-peer decisions instead of a central orchestrator.Three mechanisms carry the design: a weighted directed graph whose edges are updated after each task and pruned below a threshold (Section 3.2, Eqs. 2 and 3); a per-agent RAG memory of local trajectory fragments, retrieved top-k at inference and pruned when the pool hits capacity (Section 3.3, Eq. 4); and a routing step where an agent may forward a task, split it, or execute it, with capability vectors updated from observed performance (Section 3.4).The empirical case rests on Table 1 (three backbones -DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen-turbo -across MATH, BBH, and API-Bank, with nine baselines), Table 2 (heterogeneity on BBH), Table 3 (evolution ablation), and Figures 5, 8, 9, 10.The framing questions -can specialization emerge without a controller, and does decentralized routing buy anything -are good ones, and the routing/memory design is described in enough detail to be argued with.My problem is with what the experiments actually establish.The headline claims that the abstract makes loudestfault tolerance, privacy preservation, scalability, ef ciency -are the ones with no measurement behind them at all, and several accuracy numbers in the tables do not survive arithmetic checking. Does the claim hold on the dataPartly, and not for the claims the paper leads with.Take them one at a time.Accuracy.Section 4.2 (line following Table 1) says AgentNet "consistently outperforms centralized frameworks." On the GPT-4o-mini block of Table 1, it does not outperform them: AgentNet's MATH column reads 85.00, the same value as AFLOW and as GPTSwarm in the same block; AgentNet's BBH Qeios qeios.com

title: Kaifeng Prefecture: A Safe-Harness Architecture for Preventing Autonomous LLM-Agent Attacks
abstract: As autonomous large language model (LLM) agents gain tool-use and long-horizon planning capabilities, they present a growing risk of executing harmful actions without explicit human authorization. Existing safety measures—such as alignment training, prompt hardening, and execution-time moderation—often fail against multi-step adversarial strategies in which an initially benign request is progressively transformed into a dangerous outcome. We introduce Kaifeng Prefecture, a safe-harness architecture that prevents autonomous LLM-agent attacks through structural separation of roles and control-flow inversion. The architecture assigns evaluative, observational, predictive, and capability functions to distinct modules (Value Judge, Observer, Predictor, and Capability), routes high-risk actions through an external gate, and preserves a human interrupt channel. Three formal propositions and accompanying floor invariants characterize the conditions under which harmful commands are blocked before execution. To make the design concrete, we describe a 23-scenario prototype implemented with a TranscriptBackend, demonstrating how the harness intercepts and neutralizes attack chains that bypass conventional guardrails. The result is a safety architecture that limits the autonomy of LLM agents without requiring full symbolic verification of every possible plan.

title: Kaifeng Prefecture: A Safe-Harness Architecture for Preventing Autonomous LLM-Agent Attacks
abstract: As autonomous large language model (LLM) agents gain tool-use and long-horizon planning capabilities, they present a growing risk of executing harmful actions without explicit human authorization.
